source.title: MedCoG: Maximizing LLM Inference Density in Medical Reasoning via Meta-Cognitive Regulation
source.authors: Yu Zhao; Hao Guan; Yongcheng Jing; Ying Zhang; Dacheng Tao

record.file_problem: None noted; the paper and its appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study fits and analyzes accuracy against inference cost on medical reasoning benchmarks, a different scaling setup from pretraining size, tokens, and compute.
record.gate_note: The study tests inference-time cost versus downstream accuracy, not held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, training tokens, or training compute. Other reported strategy accuracies and IIE comparisons do not test the listed scaling versions.
record.test_reason: The study fits a logarithmic accuracy-versus-inference-cost curve across prompting and agent methods. All methods run on one fixed backbone (GPT-4o), with accuracy and cost taken from MedAgentsBench. It uses this curve as a reference to compute its own metric, Inference Density, for MedCoG. Nothing varies model parameters, training tokens, training compute or pretraining loss. V6 concerns downstream gains with model scale or pretraining loss, not with per-sample spending across different methods. The fitting-function check (Appendix G) concerns this inference-cost curve, not pretraining scaling laws, so it does not bear on V7. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that existing medical reasoning methods follow a logarithmic inference-cost scaling curve with diminishing returns. They find that MedCoG's meta-cognitive regulation reaches 6.2× Inference Density and the highest IIE, and that an Oracle strategy selector shows a much higher upper bound. They also find that backbones differ in meta-cognitive characteristics.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes inference-time cost and medical-task accuracy using a logarithmic fit; it does not measure pretraining loss across parameter, token, or training-compute scales.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted curve’s quality and interpretability depend on the fitting function; the authors report a lower R² for linear fitting and degenerate density estimates for power-law fitting in some cases.

fits_no_version.finding: Across existing prompting and agent methods on GPT-4o (five hard medical sets), the Pareto frontier of accuracy versus per-sample cost fits a logarithmic curve with R²=0.996. Gains shrink as cost rises. Linear fits give lower R², and power-law fits give comparable R² (Appendix G).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time accuracy across test-time reasoning methods on a fixed LLM rises roughly logarithmically with per-sample inference cost.

fits_no_version.finding: Meta-cognitive monitor F1 improves from Qwen3-8B (Knowledge Density F1 0.33) to Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-Max (0.80, 0.79). Authors say larger models give more reliable monitoring.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM self-assessment (meta-cognitive monitoring) quality improves with model size.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The scaling analysis uses inference costs and benchmark results for five hard medical sets, with GPT-4o-based methods; no uncertainty estimates are reported for the fitted curve. Baseline accuracy and cost results are described as reported in MedAgentsBench.
record.rows_left_out: No other scaling-curve results were left out. The paper’s strategy accuracy and IIE comparisons were not extracted as scaling rows because they do not measure the claim versions’ stated pretraining scaling quantities or downstream predictability against model size/pretraining loss.

untested.parts: All: no pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no extrapolation from small to large training runs.
All: no other modality or training regime scaling.
All: no downstream performance versus model scale or pretraining loss. The axis is inference cost across methods on a fixed backbone.
All: no pretraining-law exponents or compute-optimal splits are fitted or compared.

record.verdict_notes: The 'inference scaling law' here is a curve across different methods' costs at fixed model size, so it does not bear on the pretraining scaling-law versions. The reader's V6 and V7 links and labels are removed. Baseline accuracy and cost come from MedAgentsBench. No uncertainty is reported for the fit.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or training compute.
Prediction of much larger pretraining runs from smaller runs.
Compute-optimal allocation between model parameters and training tokens.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Scaling laws in other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study tests inference-cost trends on medical benchmarks, not scaling with model size or pretraining loss.

It examines fitting-function sensitivity for an inference-cost curve, but not pretraining exponents, compute-optimal parameter/token splits, disagreements between published pretraining laws, or departures across pretraining scales.

rows.subject: Pareto frontier of existing approaches (reference methods; GPT-4o backbone)
rows.operation_detail: Fit accuracy against inference cost for existing methods on five hard medical benchmark sets.
rows.measure: Fit of downstream accuracy versus inference cost
rows.value: R² = 0.996; the authors state most approaches align largely with a logarithmic inference scaling curve, with progressively smaller performance gains as cost increases.
rows.note: This is inference-time cost scaling, not pretraining loss scaling.
rows.check: The axis is per-sample API cost across different reasoning methods on a fixed GPT-4o backbone, not model scale or pretraining loss. It measures a different construct from V6. The R²=0.996 is a fit to the baselines' Pareto frontier (a selected subset of methods), with accuracies from MedAgentsBench. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Reference Pareto frontier of existing approaches
rows.operation_detail: Refit the reference frontier using a linear function.
rows.value: Lower R² than the logarithmic fit; exact value not stated.
rows.note: The comparison shows fit quality varies by fitting function; no exact R² is given.
rows.check: This is fit-function sensitivity for the inference-cost reference curve, not for pretraining scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits. No R² value is given. It does not bear on V7.

rows.subject: Reference Pareto frontier of existing approaches
rows.operation_detail: Refit the reference frontier using a power-law function.
rows.measure: Fit quality and interpretability of density estimates
rows.value: Comparable R²; density estimates become degenerate when model accuracy exceeds the function’s asymptote.
rows.note: The authors report a fitting-choice limitation, not a test of pretraining power-law exponents.
rows.check: Same as R2. The power-law refit of an inference-cost curve has 'comparable R²' with no number and does not bear on V7.

rows.subject: MedCoG-META
rows.operation_detail: Recalculate inference density under alternative fitted scaling curves.
rows.value: Greater than 2× across all fitting variants and all five hard sets.
rows.note: The authors say the efficiency conclusion remains high across the tested fitting variants.
rows.check: This is the study's own method's Inference Density compared against the reference curve, a robustness check of their own metric. It should not be linked to a version. It is better treated as an own-method result, not a claim row.

rows.subject: MedCoG-META
rows.operation_detail: Compare actual inference cost with the cost projected by the reference logarithmic curve at the same accuracy.

conditions.value: existing methods on the baseline Pareto frontier

rows.note: This reports relative inference efficiency, not a version’s named measure of downstream predictability.
rows.check: This is the study's own method's performance metric (6.2× density), not a measure of any version. Correctly unlinked.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
